title: Design a distributed cache (Redis / Memcached)
relevance: High — classic infra HLD prompt ("design Redis/Memcached") and the deep-dive that follows almost every read-heavy product design; campus + experienced; FAANG and Indian product cos.
company_notes: Campus/intern/new-grad: frequent as "add Redis" inside URL shortener, feed, e-commerce; standalone distributed-cache design at stronger campuses and infra-leaning loops. Experienced (1–4+ YOE): consistent hashing/slots, replication failover, hot keys, stampede, client vs proxy, Facebook memcache paper depth — Meta, Amazon, Google, Uber, LinkedIn, Atlassian, Flipkart, etc. Very high as a building block; high as standalone where large cache fleets run. Pair with h03_caching + h15 before mocks.

phases.goal: Clarify cache-product vs app+cache, lock GET/SET/DELETE+TTL+LRU, NFRs, and out-of-scope durability/consistency.

must_hit.point: Functional core: GET(key)→value or miss; SET(key,value,ttl?) with optional expiry; DELETE(key); evict by LRU when memory is full
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names GET/SET/DELETE, optional TTL on SET, and LRU as the default full-memory eviction policy

must_hit.point: NFRs: low-latency hits (< ~1–10 ms in-region; often < 10 ms), high availability, eventual consistency OK across replicas, horizontal scale for memory + QPS
must_hit.evidence_hint: States sub-~10 ms hit latency, HA, eventual consistency across replicas, and scale-out for RAM and ops/s

must_hit.point: Clarify first: KV only? TTL? eviction? durability? strong vs eventual consistency? read/write ratio? smart client hashing? and whether they want the cache cluster or app+cache-aside
must_hit.evidence_hint: Asks the clarify list and defaults to designing the cache cluster while naming cache-aside as the client pattern

must_hit.point: Out of scope unless asked: disk durability as primary store, SQL, cross-DC strong consistency, multi-key ACID, rich query
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly draws the line excluding durable primary store, SQL, cross-DC strong consistency, and multi-key ACID

probes: What are the functional and non-functional requirements for this distributed cache, and what are you deliberately leaving out of scope?

hints.1: Start by asking whether they want a Redis-like cache product or app-side caching in front of a DB.
hints.2: Lock GET/SET/DELETE + optional TTL + LRU, then latency/HA/eventual consistency and scale assumptions.
hints.3: Say: GET/SET/DELETE with optional TTL and LRU; hits < ~1–10 ms; HA with eventual consistency; scale ~1 TB / ~100k–1M ops/s; out of scope: durable primary, SQL, cross-DC strong consistency, multi-key ACID.

phases.goal: Size the working set and shards so hit rate and miss tax to the DB are explicit.

must_hit.point: Working-set math: e.g. 1B keys × ~1 KB ≈ 1 TB on disk DB, but ~10% of keys serve ~90% traffic → ~100 GB in RAM for high hit rate
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates full DB size (~1 TB) from hot working set (~100 GB from ~10% of keys)

must_hit.point: Capacity: peak QPS ~100k–1M ops/s; per-node RAM e.g. 16–64 GB usable → ~2–10+ shards for 100 GB plus headroom for overhead/replicas
must_hit.evidence_hint: Picks a QPS band in 100k–1M and derives multi-shard count from 16–64 GB nodes for ~100 GB working set

must_hit.point: Per-node QPS: one Redis primary often 50k–100k+ simple ops/s → shard for QPS and memory
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites ~50k–100k+ ops/s per primary as order-of-magnitude and says sharding covers both RAM and QPS

must_hit.point: Miss tax: at 99% hit + 1M QPS → 10k DB reads/s steady; one dead shard doubles miss load for its keys — size the DB for the cold case; hit rate is an economics problem
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks 99% hit at 1M QPS → 10k DB reads/s and notes a dead shard spikes misses so the DB must absorb the cold case

probes: How large is the working set versus the full dataset, and how many shards do you need for memory and QPS?

hints.1: Estimate hot keys in RAM, not the entire database size.
hints.2: Use ~10% hot keys → ~100 GB, then divide by per-node usable RAM and check per-primary QPS.
hints.3: Say: 1B×~1 KB≈1 TB DB but ~100 GB hot; 16–64 GB nodes → ~2–10+ shards; 100k–1M QPS with ~50k–100k+/primary; 99% hit at 1M QPS → 10k DB reads/s.

phases.goal: Sketch the cache protocol (and optionally cache-aside around domain reads/writes).

must_hit.point: Cache protocol: GET key → HIT value | MISS; SET key value [EX seconds]; DELETE key
must_hit.evidence_hint: Writes the three ops with HIT/MISS on GET and optional EX seconds on SET

must_hit.point: Optional admin/cluster ops: add/remove node, rebalance slots, stats (INFO, hit ratio, memory)
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions membership/rebalance and observability stats beyond the data plane API

must_hit.point: If app API: cache-aside getUser loads cache then DB then SET with TTL; updateUser saves DB then DELETE key to invalidate
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows miss-path SET after DB load and write-path DB-first then DELETE for invalidation

probes: What does the cache interface look like, and how would an application use it on read and write?

hints.1: This is a cache protocol, not a public REST product—keep it to key-value ops.
hints.2: Sketch GET/SET/DELETE first; if they want the app, show cache-aside + delete-on-write.
hints.3: Say: GET→HIT|MISS, SET with optional EX, DELETE; app pattern is GET miss→DB→SET(ttl), and update is DB save then DELETE key.

phases.goal: Define per-entry fields and node-local plus cluster metadata structures.

must_hit.point: Per entry in memory: key (string/bytes, namespace prefixes like user:123), value (opaque bytes or Redis type), expire_at (absolute time; lazy + active expiry), lru_node (pointer into LRU list / approximated LRU sample)
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists key, value, expire_at, and lru_node with namespace and lazy/active expiry notes

must_hit.point: Node-local structures: hash map key→entry; doubly linked list (or Redis approximated LRU) for eviction order; optional TTL min-heap / timing wheel
must_hit.evidence_hint: Draws map + LRU list and mentions optional TTL heap/timing wheel

must_hit.point: Cluster metadata: node list / slot map (or consistent-hash ring + vnodes); primary–replica membership
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names routing metadata (slots or ring+vnodes) and primary–replica membership

probes: What do you store per cache entry, and what data structures live on each node versus in cluster metadata?

hints.1: Separate the in-memory entry fields from the cluster membership/routing map.
hints.2: Entry = key/value/expire_at/lru_node; node = hash map + LRU (+ TTL structure); cluster = slots/ring + primary/replica.
hints.3: Say: entry has key, value, expire_at, lru_node; node has map + doubly linked LRU and optional TTL heap; cluster holds slot/ring map and primary–replica membership.

phases.goal: Assemble sharded cache primaries, async replicas, client routing, config service, and DB as source of truth.

must_hit.point: Default shape: app servers with client lib (hash(key)/slot map) → cache shard primaries; each primary owns a key range/slots; in-memory KV + LRU + TTL
must_hit.evidence_hint: Draws client-side routing to sharded primaries that hold in-memory KV with LRU+TTL

must_hit.point: HA: async replicate to replicas; promote on failure via Sentinel / Cluster / config service; unreplicated writes can become misses and refill from DB
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows primary→async replicas, failover via Sentinel/Cluster/config, and miss-refill after lost writes

must_hit.point: Routing choices: client-side hashing (Memcached/Facebook — lowest latency); proxy (mcrouter/Twemproxy — dumb clients, extra hop); server redirects (Redis Cluster MOVED/ASK) — pick one and name the tradeoff
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares client-side vs proxy vs MOVED/ASK and states which they pick with a latency/ops tradeoff

must_hit.point: Config/membership (ZK, Consul, Redis Cluster bus, Sentinel) publishes membership so clients avoid dead nodes; DB is source of truth on miss/after invalidate; alternative: co-located cache on app hosts vs dedicated fleet
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names a config/membership plane, DB as SoT on miss, and co-located vs dedicated cache fleet

probes: Walk through the high-level components: how do clients reach the right shard, and how do you handle failover?

hints.1: Think app → routing → shard primary → replica, plus a membership service and the DB behind misses.
hints.2: Prefer client-side consistent hashing or slot map; add async replicas and a config plane for membership.
hints.3: Say: smart clients hash to primaries; async replicas + Sentinel/Cluster/config for promote; unreplicated loss → miss→DB; optional proxy when many languages need central policy.

phases.goal: Probe sharding remapping, invalidation consistency, routing, and hot-key/stampede mitigations.

must_hit.point: Sharding: hash % N remaps almost everything on scale-out (miss storm); consistent hashing + vnodes remaps ~1/N keys; Redis Cluster uses fixed 16384 hash slots (CRC16(key) mod 16384), not a classic ring — same goal, different mechanism
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts mod-N remapping with ~1/N consistent-hash moves and correctly names Redis 16384 slots

must_hit.point: Consistency/invalidation: cache may be stale within TTL/invalidate contract; prefer DB write then DELETE key (idempotent) over updating cache in place; async replication → brief stale reads after failover OK for most caches
must_hit.evidence_hint: States TTL/invalidate staleness, DB-first then DELETE, and accepts brief post-failover stale reads

must_hit.point: Client routing vs proxy: client hash saves +1 RTT but harder client upgrades; proxy (mcrouter) centralizes routing/pooling/shadow-warmup at +latency and ops complexity
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names RTT vs upgrade cost for clients and central policy vs extra hop for proxy

must_hit.point: Hot keys & stampedes: hot reads → L1, replicate hot key to N nodes, split subkeys, or mcrouter-style pools; stampede → lease/single-flight, probabilistic early refresh, jittered TTLs, serve-stale-while-revalidate; hot writes often need key redesign
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives at least one hot-read mitigation and one stampede mitigation, and notes hot writes need redesign

probes: What happens when you add a cache node, and how do you handle hot keys and expiry stampedes?

hints.1: Interviewers usually dig into remapping, invalidation order, and hot keys next.
hints.2: Compare mod hash vs consistent hashing/vnodes vs 16384 slots, then DB-first DELETE, then lease/L1 for herds.
hints.3: Say: avoid hash%N miss storms—use consistent hashing (~1/N move) or Redis 16384 slots; DB write then DELETE; hot key via L1/replicate/split; stampede via lease/single-flight or jittered TTL.

phases.goal: Show how memory, QPS, fan-out, failure, and cold start scale—and what sharding cannot fix.

must_hit.point: Memory: add shards and rebalance slots/ring; size for working set + replica copies; QPS/CPU on one primary: more shards, but for hot keys use replication or L1 — sharding alone will not help one viral key
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates scale-out for capacity from hot-key mitigations that sharding cannot fix

must_hit.point: Node failure: promote replica; clients refresh map; temporary miss spike — DB must absorb ~traffic/N extra; cold cluster/deploy: warmup, shadow traffic (mcrouter), or accept miss storm with shedding
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes promote + map refresh, DB absorbing ~traffic/N, and warmup/shadow/shedding for cold start

must_hit.point: Network fan-out: one page may touch hundreds of keys → batch/multiget, connection pooling, avoid thundering incast
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites multi-key page fan-out and answers with multiget/batching and pooling

must_hit.point: Multi-region: usually per-region cache + invalidate or TTL; global exact cache coherence is rarely worth it
must_hit.evidence_hint: Chooses per-region caches with invalidate/TTL over global exact coherence

probes: Where does this system bottleneck under load or failure, and what does not get fixed by adding more shards?

hints.1: Separate capacity bottlenecks from single-key and failure-induced miss storms.
hints.2: Cover memory/QPS scale-out, hot-key limits, DB absorbing ~traffic/N on shard death, and multiget for fan-out.
hints.3: Say: add shards for RAM/QPS; L1/replicate for hot keys; on failure DB takes ~traffic/N extra; batch/multiget for hundreds of keys; per-region cache + TTL/invalidate.

tradeoffs.topic: hash % N vs consistent hashing (+ vnodes) vs Redis 16384 slots
tradeoffs.strong_answer: hash % N is simple until scale-out remaps almost all keys and causes a miss storm; consistent hashing with vnodes keeps remapping to ~1/N and evens load; Redis Cluster instead moves fixed 16384 slots between nodes (CRC16(key) mod 16384)—same minimal-remap goal, not a classic ring.

tradeoffs.topic: client-side hashing vs proxy (mcrouter/Twemproxy) vs server redirects
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Client-side hashing/slot map saves a hop and is lowest latency (Memcached/Facebook style) but upgrades are harder; a proxy gives dumb clients central routing, pooling, and shadow/warmup at extra latency and ops cost; Redis Cluster MOVED/ASK redirects push topology awareness to servers—pick one and name the latency vs ops tradeoff.

tradeoffs.topic: cache-aside delete-on-write vs updating the cache in place
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Prefer DB write then DELETE key (idempotent invalidate) plus TTL; updating the cache before/instead of a committed DB write risks fill/invalidate races and phantoms after crashes; async replica lag means brief stale reads after failover, which is acceptable for most caches.

Memcached is simple GET/SET, multi-threaded, no rich types—good for dumb high-QPS cache; Redis adds structures, scripting, optional persistence, Sentinel/Cluster and is the default interview pick unless they explicitly want a multi-threaded simple cache.

gotchas.trap: Just use hash % N for sharding
gotchas.correction: Adding a node remaps almost everything → mass miss storm; use consistent hashing (+ vnodes) or Redis 16384 slots so only a fraction of keys move.
Uneven arcs create hot nodes; add virtual nodes for even load.

gotchas.trap: Saying Redis uses a consistent-hash ring
gotchas.correction: Redis Cluster uses fixed 16384 hash slots (CRC16(key) mod 16384), not a classic ring—same interview story, different mechanism.

gotchas.trap: Updating the cache before the DB commit
gotchas.correction: A crash can leave phantom values; fix is DB-first then invalidate (DELETE) the key.

gotchas.trap: Ignoring thundering herd on popular key TTL expiry
gotchas.correction: Use lease/single-flight, probabilistic early refresh, jittered TTLs, or serve-stale-while-revalidate.

gotchas.trap: Treating the cache as a durable store (write-back without acknowledging loss)
gotchas.correction: Cache is a lossy accelerator; unreplicated or write-back data can disappear—source of truth is usually the DB; prefer availability + eventual consistency unless durability is required.

gotchas.trap: More shards will fix a hot key
gotchas.correction: One key still maps to one shard; need L1, replicate the hot key, or split keys—sharding alone will not help.

gotchas.trap: Redis down: silently fall through to Postgres with no protection
gotchas.correction: Fail-open with load shedding, a small local fallback, or a circuit breaker so a cache outage does not melt the DB.
